system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2169-01-08 22:32:00 to 2169-01-09 14:46:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with long-standing type 1 diabetes and multiple complications, including neuropathy, gastroparesis, and chronic foot ulcers, was admitted for worsening bilateral foot infections. She presented with uncontrolled blood sugars, leukocytosis, and acute kidney injury likely due to dehydration and infection. She underwent debridement of both foot ulcers, with negative pressure wound therapy applied to the right foot. Cultures grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Group B Streptococcus, and she was treated with targeted IV antibiotics, later transitioned to oral doxycycline and levofloxacin. Her infection resolved, renal function improved, and blood glucose stabilized on a revised insulin regimen. She was discharged to extended care with wound care instructions, non-weight-bearing status on the right foot, and plans for close podiatry follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You came in because your potassium was high during a routine check with your nurse. How are you feeling tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay, actually. No chest pain or anything. But I was surprised when they told me to come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good, I’m glad you’re not having symptoms. High potassium can be dangerous, but we caught it early. Your level was 6.2, which is elevated. We’ve given you some insulin to help bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Is that why I’ve been feeling a bit off lately? I’ve been drinking less water because it’s hard to get up and move around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could definitely play a role. Your kidney function was a little worse than usual—creatinine was 2.2, up from your baseline of 1.8. That, plus the Losartan you’re on, may have contributed to the high potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Losartan? That’s for my blood pressure, right? Should I stop taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve stopped it for now. It’s an excellent blood pressure med, but it can raise potassium, especially when kidney function dips. Your blood pressure is still well-controlled, so we’re safe to hold it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my diabetes? I skipped a dose of insulin yesterday because I wasn’t feeling well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar was high when you arrived—358—but not dangerously so. We’ve kept you on your usual insulin: NPH in the morning, Lantus instead of Levemir while you’re here, and a sliding scale for corrections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my foot ulcers? I’ve been changing the dressings every day like they told me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Podiatry checked them earlier. They said the wounds are healing well, no signs of infection. You’re still on doxycycline and levofloxacin—keep taking those until the full course is done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good, I was worried about that. And my stomach—sometimes I feel full quickly and don’t eat much. Could that be why I’m dehydrated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Gastroparesis can reduce your fluid intake. We’ve started IV fluids—2 liters of normal saline—to help rehydrate you. That should also help your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning look much better. Potassium is down to 5.2, and your creatinine is back to your baseline of 1.8.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you later this morning. We’ll stop the IV fluids, and you’ll go home on your regular meds except Losartan, which we’ve discontinued.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I need to follow up with my PCP?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll have a potassium check soon—your PCP will schedule it. They’ll also monitor your blood pressure and decide if you need a different medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to do that. And keep up with the foot care and antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Continue the doxycycline and levofloxacin as prescribed, keep the wounds clean and dry, and attend your podiatry follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And stay hydrated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. Drink regularly, even if you don’t feel like it. That will help your kidneys and prevent high potassium from coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are ready. We’ve scheduled your lab work for potassium and basic metabolic panel. Make sure to fax the results to your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for explaining everything. I feel much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have a nurse go over your discharge instructions one more time, and then you can head home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to manage on my own at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re alert and independent. Home health will assist with wound care, and you’re already doing a great job with your diabetes and medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll follow all the instructions.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with long-standing type 1 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, gastroparesis, and bilateral foot ulcers was admitted for asymptomatic hyperkalemia with a potassium level of 6.2. The elevation was likely due to recent up-titration of losartan and mild acute kidney injury from reduced oral intake. She received intravenous insulin and fluids, which normalized her potassium and renal function. Her foot ulcers were healing well on continued oral antibiotics, and her blood glucose was stabilized on her home insulin regimen. Losartan was discontinued, and she was discharged home with instructions to follow up with her primary care provider for blood pressure management and repeat potassium monitoring.
